Description of Wastewater and Biosolids Treatment and Controls The Discharger owns and operates a wastewater collection, treatment, and disposal facility, which provides service to the community of Summerland. The Facility receives domestic and commercial wastewater and currently serves approximately 480 connections. ATTACHMENT F – FACT SHEET F-4 [Page 85] SUMMERLAND SANITARY DISTRICT ORDER NO. R3-2022-0014 WASTEWATER TREATMENT PLANT NPDES NO. CA0048054 The collection system is composed of approximately 8.7 miles of sewer main and 3 lift stations. The existing treatment plant has been in operation since 1958 and is considered a tertiary treatment facility. The treatment system consists of a grinder and bar screen at headworks, a flow equalization basin, primary clarifier, two activated sludge aeration basins, two secondary clarifiers, a chlorine contact chamber, anthracite bed filter, and dechlorination. Wastewater is discharged via a 740-foot ocean outfall at Discharge Point 001 to the Pacific Ocean, a water of the United States. The minimum initial dilution ratio of seawater to effluent is 60:1. Biosolids are managed in two aerobic digesters, dewatered by a two-meter belt press, and stockpiled in a sludge holding bed. The holding bed contains drains which permit leachate to flow back to the head of the liquid treatment train for treatment. chunks.text: The present model considers the wastewater input capacity of 800 Ml/day. The designed wastewater treatment system includes the primary treatment process of grit subtraction and sludge sedimentation, secondary treatment system of activated sludge process with sludge removal via sedimentation, and tertiary treatment of the treated water for microalgae cultivation. In addition, sludge stabilisation is carried out via the anaerobic digestion process. This process has been modelled based on the modified large-scale Melbourne's municipal sewage treatment plant adapting microalgae tertiary treatment described in The American Society of Civil Engineers (ASCE) and Water Environmental Federation (WEF) (1998) (Batten et al., 2013) . The process flow diagram of the wastewater treatment system is described in Fig. 2a . The wastewater is considered as moderately polluted wastewater and its inorganic nutrient composition is shown in Supplementary information. The primary stage of wastewater treatment is the removal of both grit and primary sludge. Grit is represented in the model as solid-state silicon dioxide which is about 1% of the total inlet water flow.

chunks.text: Primary sedimentation is to remove the suspended solids (SS) by controlling the water flow velocity. It is required the settling time of SS shorter than the water travelling time in the tank. The SS with low density (1.1 g/mL and 1.5 g/mL) or small size but high density (1.5 g/mL) is the target pollutants to be removed in primary clarification. Most abundant MPs in the wastewater is PET followed by PE and PP (Fig. 2b ). The density of PET is between 0.96 and 1.45 g/mL. It is predicted that the primary sedimentation would catch the MPs consist of PET. However, PE and PP are difficult to be removed as they have density lower than water. Hence, wastewater containing large amount of moderate-density MPs would have high MPs removal during primary treatment.

chunks.text: The secondary clarifier is a 10-layer non-reactive system labelled from the bottom to the top. It has a total height of 4 m, and occupies a surface area of 1500 m 2 and a volume of 6000 m 3 . The tank is fed from the 6th, treated water is harvested from the 10th, and the settled sludge flows out from the first layer. A fraction of the sludge flows out of the system in the form of waste at a flow rate of 385 m 3 /d, corresponding to a biomass age of 9 days, while the other fraction is recycled externally to the first tank at a rate of 18,446 m 3 /d. The biological processes occurring in both biological reactors are simulated using the IWA Activated Sludge Model No. 1 (ASM1) proposed by [47] . This model uses thirteen state variables to track the fate of biodegradable, non-biodegradable, soluble, insoluble, nitrogen, and carbon materials. These state variables are linked to eight degradation bioprocesses occurring in biological reactors.

chunks.text: A pilot-scale system, consisting of a grit tank and microscreen for primary treatment followed by a SAF-MBR 2.0 for secondary treatment, was installed at the Codiga Resource Recovery Center (Stanford, CA), as illustrated in. The pilot-scale system treated municipal wastewater pumped from the Serra Street sewer on the Stanford campus for more than three years. Sewage was de-gritted in a grit tank then subject to primary treatment by screening through a 0.3 mm pore size microscreen (MS-28, Hydro International). The pilot-scale SAF-MBR 2.0 consisted of: (1) two AFBRs operated in parallel, hereafter referred to as AFBR 1 and AFBR 2, containing fluidized GAC biocarrier, and (2) a gas-sparged membrane tank equipped with ultrafiltration membranes. Recirculation of bulk fluid (twice the influent flow rate) between the three reactors enabled complete mixing and control of solids accumulation within the gas-sparged membrane tank.

chunks.text: Electrochemical treatment systems have been shown to provide effective treatment of latrine wastewater. Greater than 5-log inactivation of bacterial and viral indicator organisms is achieved via production of reactive chlorine species from chloride (15−20 mM) within 1 h at 4 V applied cell potential. 3 A combination of reactive chlorine species and direct oxidation provide reduction of chemical oxygen demand (COD) 4 and transformation of trace organic contaminants within 4 h (3.5− 4.5 V applied cell potential) 5−7 with rates enhanced at elevated chloride concentrations (up to 75 mM). Under similar operating conditions, ammonium removal occurs via breakpoint chlorination, 8 and phosphorus can be precipitated as hydroxyapatite. 9 Unfortunately, strongly oxidizing conditions in the presence of the high concentrations of chloride and organic matter typical of latrine wastewater also result in formation of toxic byproducts. 10 While wastewater disinfection is essential to protecting human health, an ideal electrochemical system should also be designed to minimize toxic byproduct formation. 11 Chloride enhances electrochemical treatment via formation of reactive chlorine species (e.g., hypochlorous acid, chloramines, and chlorine radicals).

Some systems have slightly different configurations (e.g., inclusion of primary treatment); however, the configurations shown were typical of most sites in the study. Use of biosolid dewatering varied across sites with some utilizing belt filter presses, some others utilizing drying beds, and several not utilizing any form at all. The main difference among technologies is the secondary treatment, where OD and EA use different reactor configurations in conjunction with a clarifier for treatment and SBRs use multiple basins for aeration and settling. chunks.text: Preliminary treatment is the initial stage where coarse particles and foreign matter commonly found in raw wastewater are removed to optimize subsequent treatment processes (Sonune and Ghate, 2004) . This stage involves activities such as coarse screening, grit removal, and the comminution of large objects in wastewater. Grit chambers maintain high water velocities, preventing organic compounds from settling within the chamber. Although not all wastewater treatment plants incorporate grit removal in their preliminary treatment, some employ comminutors alongside coarse screening to reduce the size of large particles. Additionally, flow measurement devices and wave flumes are commonly used during this phase (Pachwarya et al., 2021) . It's crucial to remove oil and grease from wastewater at this stage to mitigate its adverse effects on the subsequent treatment processes. This is typically achieved through methods such as chlorination, vacuum flotation, and aeration (Pachwarya et al., 2021) .

Specifically, plants A, B, and C experienced a reduction in CFP of 7.55%, 9.5%, and 10.59%, respectively. This is because greater particulate settling in the primary clarifier results in lower CO 2 emissions from microbial respiration and higher waste sludge  contents in the AD process (Gori et al., 2011 (Gori et al., , 2013)) . In terms of CO 2 emissions, the AD ranked third after PG, with 0.019, 0.039, and 0.34 kg CO 2 /kg COD rem. for plants A, B, and C, respectively. However, the incoming COD concentration to the AD of each system was significantly different. Plant C received almost 5.6 times lower COD than plant A, resulting in higher COD removal (78.75%) and concurrently larger CO 2 emissions.

chunks.text: The secondary biological treatment consists of two carrousel-shaped biological reactors with suspended biomass, equipped with two horizontal aerators, which include nitrogen removal. Regarding the sludge line, a fraction of the solids settled in the secondary settler is purged to the sludge thickener. Previously to the band filter, the sludge passes through a homogenizer to be mixed with cationic polyelectrolyte and further dewatered in the band filter prior being stored in a silo. Calafell WWTP was built on 1994 to treat the wastewaters of the municipalities of Calafell and Bellveí and designed for 70,000 population equivalent with a maximum flow of 12,000 m 3 /day. After a primary treatment, wastewater is treated in two activated sludge reactors with extended aeration including nitrogen removal, followed by the secondary settler. From these units, the treated wastewater is directly discharged to the submarine sewage. Some differences are observed in the operation of the plant between winter and summer seasons due to fluctuations on the population and changes on the influent composition. A coagulation-flocculation treatment, only operated during summer, receives the wastewater after the screening step.
